evidence_note: This pack is the Japanese reception layer that the T1299 pack declared missing. Its controlling witness is a modern scholarly article read directly in a hash-pinned PDF, not a primary Japanese manuscript, so its rules are grade B: they report what a specialist says the primary Japanese record contains, with the primary citations he gives carried through verbatim so a reviewer can go to them. Two of its claims - the Futian li epoch and the internal consistency of two dated horoscopes' elapsed-day counts - were recomputed here rather than taken on the article's word, and both close. The single most consequential correction this pack makes is that the birth-mansion refusal in sukuyo_rule_manifest.json was justified by 'no named lunisolar regime exists'; a named, dated regime does exist and is recorded here.

scope.applies_to: the calendar regime under which a Japanese Sukuyodo birth mansion was actually derived

conditions.question: which lunisolar calendar did sukuyoshi use when they converted a birth into the lunar month and day that T1299's birth-mansion procedure requires
conditions.witness: Kotyk 2018 states without hedging that the Futian li was used by the Sukuyoshi through the Heian and Kamakura periods, citing Momo 1969, 400-408

conclusion.author: 曹士蒍 Cao Shiwei
conclusion.produced: between 780 and 783 CE, updated around 806 CE
conclusion.relation_to_this_tradition: the Qiyao rangzai jue (T1308) ephemerides were either taken from or based upon it, and it is the calendar the Japanese astrologer-monks worked in
conclusion.status_change: This retires the statement in sukuyo_rule_manifest.json rule sukuyo.natal.birth_mansion_requires_lunar_calendar that no named regime is available. A named, dated, authored regime is available. What is not available is its tables.
conclusion.still_blocked: The Futian li itself does not survive as a usable table set; it is reconstructed from later citations and from the elapsed-day counts in surviving horoscopes. The checklist row therefore stays source_gated and does not become computable.

exceptions: Kotyk reports the Futian li as the calendar of Sukuyoshi practice, not as the Japanese state calendar. The state calendar was the Senmyo reki; see sukuyo.jp.senmyo_reki_is_the_state_calendar.
The date range 780-783 with an update around 806 is Kotyk's report of a reconstruction by Takesako 2016, not a dated colophon.

scope.applies_to: the day-count epoch that Japanese Sukuyodo horoscopes reckon from

conditions.evidence_1: the Sukuyo unmei kanroku, a horoscope for a man born 15 January 1113, states that 165,428 days have elapsed since the epoch of the calendar used
conditions.evidence_2: the Sukuyo go unroku, for an individual born in 1268, states that 222,245 days have elapsed
conditions.claim_under_test: both counts should resolve to the same epoch, and that epoch should be the year 660

conclusion.cross_check: 1962168 + 222245 = 2184413 = 6 August 1268 (Julian), a birth date consistent with a subject aged 44 or 45 in 1312. The difference of the two stated counts, 222245 - 165428 = 56817 days, carries 15 January 1113 forward to exactly 6 August 1268.
conclusion.significance: Two independently transmitted Japanese documents, 200 years apart, reckon from the same day. That is a stronger witness to the regime than either document alone, and it is checkable arithmetic rather than an assertion.

exceptions: Kotyk gives the epoch as 'around 660' and does not state a day. The day 660-02-15 is this pack's arithmetic consequence of his two figures under Julian reckoning, not a figure he reports.
The 1268 birth date 6 August 1268 is likewise derived here, not reported. It is offered as a consistency check on the two counts, not as a claim about that individual.
Whether the horoscopes' 'days elapsed' is inclusive or exclusive of the epoch day would shift the epoch by one day; the sources as reported do not settle it.

source_passages.work: Jeffrey Kotyk, 'Japanese Buddhist Astrology and Astral Magic: Mikkyo and Sukuyodo', Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 45/1 (2018): 37-86
source_passages.section: Horoscopy in Sukuyodo (the Sukuyo unmei kanroku)
source_passages.location: journal p. 62 (pdf_page 26): '165,428 days have elapsed since the epoch of the calendar that was used in the calculations, which indicates a start date of around 660. The year 660 is the epoch of the Futian li (Momo 1969, 404-406)'; and the parallel 222,245-day figure for the Sukuyo go unroku (Momo 1990, 142)

The two day counts were recomputed against a Julian-calendar JDN implementation in this pass; the results are recorded in the vectors.

scope.applies_to: the civil lunisolar calendar that a Japanese birth date of this period would have carried

conditions.regime: Senmyo reki 宣明暦 (Chinese Xuanming li), brought to Japan in 859 and adopted from 862
conditions.reported_complaint: around the mid-tenth century the Onmyoji Kamo no Yasunori 賀茂保憲 (917-977) held that it had been in use for well over a century and that the mainland had probably adopted a newer calendar

conclusion.role: the state calendar, i.e. the source of the civil lunar month-and-day that a Japanese birth record would state
conclusion.distinct_from: the Futian li, which is the astrologers' computational calendar
conclusion.consequence_for_the_engine: there are two named regimes in play, not one, and they are not interchangeable. A civil birth date is expressed in the Senmyo reki; the astrologer's own reckoning ran on the Futian li. Any implementation must say which it used.
conclusion.institutional_note: Sukuyoshi officially participated in state calendar production between 995 and 1038, the monk Ninso being likely the earliest to contribute from 995, and continued to argue with court calendrical experts about eclipse prediction into the thirteenth century. The two regimes were therefore in contact, not sealed off from each other.

exceptions: Kotyk names the Senmyo reki as the state calendar and as the object of Kamo no Yasunori's complaint. He does not state that sukuyoshi derived birth mansions from it, and this rule does not claim he does.
The Senmyo reki remained Japan's calendar far beyond this period; its long service life is not evidence about Sukuyodo practice specifically.

scope.applies_to: the transmission event that made horoscopy practicable in Japan

conditions.cause: Kamo no Yasunori's judgement that the Senmyo reki was stale, and his recommendation that a specialist be sent
conditions.agent: the Tendai monk Nichien 日延, disciple of Ninkan 仁観 (d. 934), himself trained in calendrical science

conclusion.destination: the state of Wuyue 吳越
conclusion.studied: a version of the Futian li together with ephemerides (licheng 立成)
conclusion.classification_note: the early Kamakura Nichu reki 二中暦 lists Nichien not as a Sukuyoshi but as a Rokumeishi 禄命師, a master of fortune telling; the first Sukuyoshi it lists is Hozo 法蔵 (905-969)
conclusion.why_it_matters: the calendar regime and the professional practice arrive as one bundle and can be dated. This is the moment at which a Japanese Sukuyodo birth mansion becomes a thing that could be computed in Japan at all.

exceptions: Kotyk notes Nichien's trip is detailed in a document dated to around 1053, roughly a century after the events.

scope.output: 本命宿 honmyo suku, the natal mansion, for a real dated birth

conditions.step_1: convert the civil birth instant into a lunar month number and lunar day (1-30) under an explicitly named regime
conditions.step_2: apply the T1299 schematic procedure encoded in sukuyo.natal.birth_mansion_primary_method and cross-checked by sukuyo.natal.birth_mansion_abbreviated_method
conditions.regime_must_be: declared in the output, dated, and bounded by a valid date range

conclusion.formula: mansion_index = (index_of_full_moon_mansion(lunar_month) + (lunar_day - 15)) mod 27, over the canonical 27-order of sukuyo.mansion.canonical_order
conclusion.engine_shape: The panel's existing multi-regime lunisolar kernel is the correct driver: compute the lunar month and day under every candidate regime, then gate. This is the same pattern as CALENDAR_REGIMES in src/engine/multitradition/ziwei.py, where a chart is computed under each plausible meridian and emitted only on agreement.
conclusion.difference_from_ziwei: the ziwei gate varies the meridian within one calendar tradition; this gate varies the calendar system itself, which is a larger disagreement and must be disclosed as such rather than presented as a timezone nicety
conclusion.status: specified, not implemented. No regime's tables are in this repository.

exceptions: The Futian li does not survive as a usable table set. Until a reconstruction is implemented and independently tested, this rule specifies a procedure that cannot be run.
The regime choice interacts with the bright/dark fortnight convention of T1299 chapter 6 (黒白月分), which is a separate unresolved question.
This rule is the schematic branch only. The observational branch is sukuyo.jp.hozo_observational_fork, and by the tradition's own adjudication the observational branch is the one that won.

scope.applies_to: the engine's disclosure and refusal behaviour when candidate regimes disagree

conditions.procedure: compute the lunar month and lunar day for the birth under every candidate regime in the declared set, then compare the resulting mansion index
conditions.candidate_set_must_be: explicit, named, dated and bounded; an empty or single-element set is a configuration choice that must itself be disclosed

conclusion.on_agreement: emit the mansion, and disclose that it was tested across the named regimes and did not move
conclusion.on_disagreement: refuse the mansion and emit the disagreement itself - each regime, its lunar date, and the mansion it would give
conclusion.rationale: the birth mansion is the anchor of the entire tradition; a wrong anchor makes every downstream relationship wrong, and the wrongness is invisible to the reader
conclusion.explicitly_a_product_choice: The sources do not say to do this. Sukuyoshi worked in one regime and did not hedge. This gate is the engine's, it is labelled configured_method, and the alternative it rejects - picking one regime silently - is named.
conclusion.prior_art_in_this_repository: src/engine/multitradition/ziwei.py CALENDAR_REGIMES computes a chart under each plausible meridian and gates the reading on agreement, refusing when the chart month moves

exceptions: Agreement across regimes is evidence of robustness, not of correctness. Two regimes can agree and both be wrong for a given birth.
This rule cannot run until at least one regime is implemented; today its only reachable branch is refusal.

scope.output: 本命宿, derived observationally rather than from the schematic table

conditions.occasion: in 961 the Sukuyoshi Hozo 法蔵 (905-969) debated the Onmyoji Kamo no Yasunori over the natal asterism of Murakami Tenno (926-967)
conditions.kamo_position: use the Xiuyao jing table assigning the 27 naksatras to the days of the lunar calendar
conditions.hozo_position: determine the natal asterism from the naksatra in which the Moon was actually lodged at the time of birth
conditions.hozo_textual_basis: the first (759) version of the Xiuyao jing states that the corresponding naksatra is always the one in which the Moon is lodged

conclusion.adjudication: a third party, Yoshino Nichizo 吉野日蔵, judged the matter in three fascicles: the natal asterism by Hozo's explanation, the ritual day by Kamo no Yasunori's explanation
conclusion.outcome: the observational derivation won and, Kotyk reports, evidently became standard in Sukuyodo - the 1113 horoscope's lunar position is not taken from the Xiuyao jing table
conclusion.fork_status: This is a genuine method fork inside the tradition and it is preserved, not averaged. The schematic table and the observed lunar longitude will disagree for real births, because T1299 itself warns that the mansions are unequal in width.
conclusion.consequence_for_the_engine: an implementation that emits only the schematic mansion is emitting the position that the tradition's own arbitration set aside for the natal question, while continuing to use Kamo's sexagenary answer for the ritual day
conclusion.recorded_dissent: Kanshin 寛信 (1084-1153) wrote that he was unaware of the basis of Hozo's conclusion, that it was not received from a teacher's instruction, and that Hozo reached it by his own views. The winning method was contested as an innovation.

exceptions: The observational branch needs a lunar longitude and a named 27-mansion boundary scheme. T1299 supplies neither; it says the mansions are wide and narrow and tells the reader to check against the sky.

Substituting a modern Jyotisha naksatra computed from a modern ephemeris is forbidden: different boundaries, different derivation, and it would silently reintroduce a 28th mansion. The refusal in sukuyo_rule_manifest.json stands.
Kotyk observes that Hozo was reasoning with Chinese lunar stations in practice while the astrological lore is Indian naksatra material; the two are not the same division of the sky.

scope.output: 本命日 honmyo nichi, the day on which the personal ritual is executed

conditions.subject_of_the_961_debate: the second point at issue alongside the natal asterism
conditions.kamo_position: Murakami Tenno was born in year 4 of Encho (926), a year that fell on hei jutsu 丙戌 in the sexagenary cycle; take hei jutsu as the ritual day
conditions.hozo_position: take the actual sexagenary day of birth, tei gai 丁亥, being the second day of the sixth lunar month

conclusion.adjudication: Yoshino Nichizo determined the ritual day by Kamo no Yasunori's explanation
conclusion.result: the ritual day is reckoned sexagenary, and on this point the Onmyodo reckoning prevailed inside a Sukuyodo consultation
conclusion.boundary_warning: This does NOT merge the two traditions and does not license any Onmyodo source in this track. It records an adjudicated split: the mansion question went to the Sukuyoshi, the day question went to the Onmyoji. The boundary rule sukuyo.boundary.sukuyodo_is_not_onmyodo is unaffected - the two remained distinct offices arguing with each other, which is the opposite of a merger.

exceptions: No sexagenary machinery may be imported into this pack from the onmyodo track on the strength of this rule. The rule records who won an argument, not a calculation this pack may run.
The two positions differ over whether the ritual day is keyed to the birth YEAR's sexagenary designation or the birth DAY's; the adjudication reportedly took the year-based answer.

scope.applies_to: the only dated, named-subject birth-mansion determination available to this track

conditions.subject: Murakami Tenno 村上天皇 (926-967)
conditions.birth: the second day of the sixth lunar month of year 4 of the reign era Encho 延長 (926); the day is tei gai 丁亥
conditions.method_applied: the Xiuyao jing table, i.e. the schematic branch this repository has already encoded
conditions.reported_result: 6/2 corresponds to Aslesa 柳, per Sukuyokyo shukusatsu 1: 13-15 as reported by Kotyk

conclusion.engine_derivation: the full-moon mansion of lunar month 6 is 女, at index 20 in the canonical 27-order; (20 + (2 - 15)) mod 27 = 7; index 7 is 柳
conclusion.significance: This is the defensibility standard's requirement 4 satisfied for this track: a dated historical consultation, with a named subject, whose stated result the encoded rules reproduce exactly. It is also a cross-witness on the encoding - it independently confirms both the month table and the canonical mansion order, since a wrong entry in either would give a different mansion.
conclusion.what_it_does_not_prove: It does not prove the schematic method is the tradition's preferred method. It reproduces the position that LOST the 961 arbitration on the natal question. That is precisely why it is useful: it shows the encoding is faithful to the table, and it shows the table is not the whole tradition.

exceptions: The result 柳 is Kotyk's report of the Japanese recension's table (Sukuyokyo shukusatsu), while this repository's encoding is from the Taisho mainland recension. The agreement is therefore also weak evidence that the two recensions agree on this table - see sukuyo.jp.japanese_recension_is_not_the_taisho_text.
No civil-date conversion is involved or claimed: the lunar month and day are given directly by the source.

scope.applies_to: the textual identity of everything this repository has encoded for this tradition

conditions.finding: Yano 2013 has demonstrated that the 'mainland recension' of the Xiuyao jing in the Taisho canon is considerably different from the 'Japanese recension'
conditions.japanese_recension: traceable to the ninth century, brought by Japanese monks, and in Kotyk's judgement best representing the original version of the text
conditions.medieval_usage: the Japanese recension 'was also exclusively used in the medieval period', which is why Kotyk cites the Sukuyokyo shukusatsu 宿曜経縮刷 (2 vols), a typeset version of the Japanese recension edited by Wakita Bunsho 脇田文紹 (1897)

conclusion.consequence: sukuyo_rule_manifest.json's 32 rules are extracted from the mainland recension. Japanese Sukuyodo practice used the other recension. The pack is therefore a faithful reading of a text that Japanese practitioners did not use in the form encoded.
conclusion.severity: This is a limitation of the same order as the missing calendar and it was not previously recorded. It is not fatal - the two recensions are versions of one work and the Murakami example agrees across them at the point tested - but no rule in this repository may be described as 'what Japanese sukuyoshi used' until the Japanese recension is collated against it.
conclusion.acquisition_target: Sukuyokyo shukusatsu, ed. Wakita Bunsho, 1897, 2 vols - an 1897 Japanese typeset edition, which is old enough that its rights position is likely favourable and which Kotyk cites by volume and page throughout

exceptions: 'Considerably different' is Kotyk's characterisation of Yano's demonstration; the specific divergences were not enumerated in the passage read, and Yano 2013 was not consulted.
The 1897 edition was not retrieved in this pass and is recorded as an acquisition target, not as a held source.

scope.applies_to: the actual shape of a Japanese Sukuyodo natal document

conditions.witness: the Sukuyo unmei kanroku 宿曜運命勘録, a horoscope with interpretation for a man born 15 January 1113, produced around 1152 when he was forty-one
conditions.second_witness: the Sukuyo go unroku 宿曜御運録, produced around 1312 for an individual born in 1268

conclusion.structure: concentric circles: the twelve earthly branches serving as the twelve Jupiter stations, the twelve zodiac signs with their planetary rulers, the positions of nine planets against the lunar stations, and an outer ring of twelve places with their auspiciousness and the branches as directional markers
conclusion.nine_planets: the seven visible bodies plus Rahu and Ketu, the latter redefined in East Asian Buddhist astrology as the lunar apogee
conclusion.why_this_matters_for_the_reading: The T1299 pack's own summary of what a Sukuyodo reading looks like - mansion-relational and calendrical, with no place doctrine - describes the Chinese source text, not the Japanese practice. Japanese Sukuyodo horoscopy is place-based and its place themes are, as Kotyk notes, largely consistent with Hellenistic doctrine, reaching East Asia through Iranian intermediaries. The defensibility spec's picture of the reading is therefore incomplete and this rule records the correction.
conclusion.precision_note: the planetary values in the 1113 horoscope use fractions and are more precise than the Qiyao rangzai jue ephemerides, and the Moon's position is not taken from the Xiuyao jing table - consistent with Hozo's observational method having become standard

exceptions: Neither horoscope was retrieved. Both are known here only through Kotyk's description and his reproduction of the 1113 chart in his figure 14.
The place names are given here as Kotyk transcribes them from the 1113 document. No delineation attached to any place is encoded, because none was read.
T1308 carries a comparable circular table but its zodiac-to-lunar-station alignment and its place names differ; the two may not be merged.

scope.applies_to: the period over which a claim about 'Sukuyodo practice' is admissible at all

conditions.before: in Hozo's own time Sukuyodo does not yet appear as an identifiable lineage or community; the -do suffix is likely in emulation of the long-established Onmyodo, and one of the first references to Sukuyodo itself is in Hozo's own report quoted in the Ono ruihi sho
conditions.after: reference to 'Sukuyo' appears in the Genji monogatari, and the first references to Sukuyodo and Sukuyoshi in aristocrats' journals date to the early-to-mid eleventh century

conclusion.emergence_window: between Hozo's death in 969 and the first or second decade of the eleventh century
conclusion.institutional_pressure: there was a tendency to exclude sukuyoshi from calendar production and court astronomy as those sciences became the professional domain of the Kamo and Abe households, which were Onmyodo
conclusion.consequence_for_this_repository: a statement of the form 'Sukuyodo held X' is only admissible with a date attached. Before roughly 1000 there is no community to hold anything; the Chinese text existed in Japan for over a century before the practice did.

exceptions: Sukuyoshi hailing primarily from Kofukuji became active among the aristocracy from the late tenth century, which slightly precedes the journal evidence; the emergence window is a range, not a date.
